system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2116-01-10 03:58:00 to 2116-01-10 11:57:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with a history of systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and alcohol abuse, was admitted with chest pain and hemoptysis. A CT scan revealed an acute pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe with associated pulmonary infarct and pleural effusion. He was started on anticoagulation with Lovenox and prescribed Coumadin for long-term management, with Pradaxa and aspirin discontinued. Despite clear explanation of the life-threatening risks, he chose to leave against medical advice. At discharge, he was alert, oriented, and demonstrated understanding of his treatment plan, including medication instructions and the need for INR monitoring. He was sent home with prescriptions and strict instructions to avoid alcohol and seek immediate care for worsening symptoms.

was continued on his home metoprolol, losartan, and lasix while 
in-house during this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You're in the hospital again. You came in coughing up blood and with chest pain. Do you remember why you're here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was at the store with my sister and started coughing blood. Then the chest pain came back. But I just want to call her—she doesn’t know I’m back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you contact her soon. First, I need to tell you—your CT scan showed a blood clot in your lung, a pulmonary embolism. It’s serious. You were given a shot for it yesterday, but you didn’t fill the prescription.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I lost the syringes. I didn’t mean to. But I feel okay now. Can’t I just go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can’t go home yet. That clot can be deadly. You need blood thinners, but we can’t send you home with them if you can’t manage the medication safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not drunk now. I only had half a beer yesterday. I can take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tox screen showed benzodiazepines, and you were agitated last night. Psychiatry saw you and said you understand the risks, so we can’t keep you against your will. But we still can’t give you the blood thinner shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? I can’t just stay here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We wanted to keep you until it was safer. But since you’re determined to leave, we’re discharging you. You’re not getting lovenox or warfarin because of the risk of bleeding, especially if you drink or fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not getting the blood thinners at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. It’s too dangerous. The clot in your lung could get worse. It’s very likely you could die if it’s not treated properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. But I can’t stay. I just need to get out of here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But please, if you start feeling worse—short of breath, chest pain, dizziness—go to the nearest hospital right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going home on your usual medicines: metoprolol, furosemide, losartan, simvastatin, sertraline, aspirin, and Pradaxa. We didn’t change anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach meds? I’ve been having heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you omeprazole for that. Also, docusate and senna if you get constipated. But no Campral while you’re still drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Can I call my sister now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll get you a phone. Just remember—this clot is life-threatening. Please take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers. You’re free to leave once you’ve spoken to your sister.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I just want to get out of here and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest is fine, but stay alert. If anything feels wrong, don’t wait—go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I don’t want to die.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That means you understand. We’re here if you need us. Please come back if you’re in trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Tell the nurse I’m ready to make that call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll be careful.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and a history of alcohol and benzodiazepine use, was re-admitted after leaving against medical advice the prior day. He presented with hemoptysis and chest pain, and imaging confirmed a pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe with likely infarct and a small to moderate pleural effusion. Despite being hemodynamically stable, he again insisted on leaving the hospital. Due to his prior failure to use prescribed anticoagulation and ongoing substance use, he was not discharged on blood thinners, as it was deemed unsafe. Psychiatry confirmed he had decision-making capacity. He was discharged home on his baseline medications with strong warnings about the life-threatening risk of untreated pulmonary embolism and instructions to seek immediate care if symptoms worsened.
